settings.hero_subtext: Answer five short steps about how your organization manages learning, and get practical priorities and next steps for the year ahead.
settings.privacy_note: Your answers are used only to generate your result. We don't ask for contact details unless you choose to share them.
settings.result_methodology: Your result is generated from predefined guidance using your responses, with adjustments for some answer combinations. Your maturity stage is self-reported, not a validated score. Treat this as a starting point for discussion.
settings.result_scope: A short, self-reported assessment of how your organization manages learning, with suggested priorities and next steps.
settings.lead_form_intro: Want to talk through your result? Leave your details and an Aptara L&D specialist will get in touch.
settings.lead_form_privacy: We'll send your name, work email, company and your assessment answers to Aptara's team through FormSubmit, a third-party form service, only to follow up on this request. We won't add you to marketing lists without asking.

questions.name: Maturity stage
questions.title: Which statement best describes how your organization manages learning today?
questions.supporting_text: A directional, self-reported stage. It adjusts how much process and governance guidance the result gives. It is never inferred from team size, sourcing or delivery format.
questions.landing_blurb: How your organization manages learning today.

answers.text: Learning is handled case by case, with limited shared processes.
Some processes and tools are established, but consistency varies.
Standard processes, ownership, and reporting are in place across most programs.

questions.name: Main challenge
questions.title: What is your main L&D challenge right now?
questions.supporting_text: Chooses the first priority, the title and the 30-day action.
questions.landing_blurb: The challenge that matters most right now.

answers.text: Keeping existing learning content accurate, relevant and up to date.
Producing and delivering learning fast enough to meet demand.
Getting people to take part in learning and apply it at work.
Keeping quality consistent across programs, teams or regions.
Showing how learning contributes to business results.

questions.title: Which learning delivery methods do you currently use?
questions.supporting_text: Multiple selections. Tailors the delivery advice; mixed delivery gets its own guidance.
questions.landing_blurb: The delivery methods you use today.

answers.text: Microlearning or performance support, such as short videos and job aids.

questions.name: Business goal
questions.title: What would you most like to improve over the next 6–12 months?
questions.supporting_text: Chooses the second priority and the 90-day action. Outcome only; never presupposes buying services.
questions.landing_blurb: What you want to improve over the next year.

A.text: Your next L&D priority: modernize priority content

B.text: Your next L&D priority: protect team capacity

C.text: Your next L&D priority: make learning easier to apply

D.text: Your next L&D priority: set shared quality standards

E.text: Your next L&D priority: connect learning to business measures

A.text: You described learning in your organization as foundational: handled case by case, with limited shared processes. That is a common starting point, and a few simple, shared ways of working can make a visible difference quickly.

B.text: You described your learning practice as developing: some processes and tools are in place, but consistency varies. The opportunity is to make what already works the standard way of working.

C.text: You described your learning practice as established, with standard processes, ownership and reporting across most programs. The focus now is less on setting things up and more on where to direct effort.

D.text: You described your learning practice as optimizing: aligned to business priorities and improved using evidence. Your next gains are likely to come from sharper measurement and from scaling what already works.

A.heading: Modernize priority content
A.text: Identify your most-used and highest-risk content and review it first for outdated information, accessibility gaps and parts you could reuse. Give each item a review date so upkeep becomes routine.
A.why: You named keeping content accurate and up to date as your main challenge.

B.heading: Protect team capacity
B.text: Make demand visible in one backlog, agree how requests are prioritized, and build reusable templates and patterns so each new program takes less effort.
B.why: You named delivering learning fast enough to meet demand as your main challenge.

C.heading: Make learning easier to apply
C.text: Design programs around the tasks people do at work, add practice and on-the-job support, and ask managers to reinforce what was learned.
C.why: You named getting people to take part in learning and apply it as your main challenge.

D.heading: Set shared quality standards
D.text: Agree a short quality checklist covering design, accuracy, accessibility and learner experience, and use it in every review, whoever builds the program.
D.why: You named keeping quality consistent across programs, teams or regions as your main challenge.

E.heading: Connect learning to business measures
E.text: For one or two priority programs, agree with the business owner which operational measure the program should influence, capture a baseline, and plan how you will review the change.
E.why: You named showing how learning contributes to business results as your main challenge.

A.heading: Increase delivery capacity
A.text: Look at where time goes today, from request to launch, and remove the biggest bottlenecks before adding more programs. Reusable designs and clear sign-off steps add capacity without adding people.
A.why: You chose increasing delivery capacity as your goal for the next 6–12 months.

B.heading: Shorten development and update time
B.text: Build a library of reusable templates, components and examples, and keep source files organized so updates are quicker to make.
B.why: You chose reducing development and update time as your goal for the next 6–12 months.

C.heading: Raise quality and consistency
C.text: Define what good looks like for your programs, share it with everyone who builds or reviews learning, and check a sample of programs against it each quarter.
C.why: You chose improving learning quality and consistency as your goal for the next 6–12 months.

D.heading: Strengthen engagement and application
D.text: Choose one program and add practice, reminders and manager follow-up after it, then compare participation and feedback with earlier runs.
D.why: You chose improving learner engagement and application as your goal for the next 6–12 months.

E.heading: Demonstrate business impact
E.text: Choose a small number of programs where a business outcome can reasonably be linked to learning, and agree with stakeholders how results will be evaluated and reported.
E.why: You chose demonstrating business impact as your goal for the next 6–12 months.

A.heading: Agree a simple intake process
A.text: Set up one shared way to request, prioritize and track learning work, with a named owner for each program. Even a lightweight process makes demand visible and decisions easier.
A.why: You said learning is handled case by case, so a shared process is the foundation the other priorities depend on.

B.heading: Standardize what already works
B.text: Pick the processes and templates that work best today and make them the default for new programs, with a short checklist for design and review.
B.why: You said consistency varies, so standardizing proven practices reduces rework without adding much overhead.

C.heading: Focus effort where it counts
C.text: Review your portfolio against current business priorities, and retire or refresh programs that no longer earn their place. Use your existing reporting to decide where to invest.
C.why: With standard processes and reporting in place, the biggest gains come from where you direct effort.

D.heading: Scale what the evidence supports
D.text: Use the evidence you already collect to find the programs with the clearest results, and apply their design patterns more widely.
D.why: You said learning is already improved using evidence, so the next step is to spread what works rather than add new process.

A.text: You deliver learning through in-person sessions. Consider which parts could be supported with short reference materials or follow-up activities, so learning continues after the session.

B.text: You deliver learning through virtual live sessions. Keep sessions interactive and focused, and add simple follow-up materials so people can revisit key points.

C.text: You use self-paced eLearning. Review your most-used modules regularly for outdated examples and accessibility gaps, and look for content you could reuse across courses.

D.text: You use microlearning and performance support. Make sure each resource is easy to find at the moment of need, and link related resources so they support a bigger goal.

E.text: You use documents and reference materials. Keep them current, easy to search and clearly owned, and consider which topics would benefit from practice or guided learning.

MULTI.text: You use several delivery methods: {Q3}. Identify where they can work together to support the same outcome, rather than planning each one separately.

A.text: You don't have a dedicated internal L&D team, so clear ownership matters most: name who decides priorities and who signs off learning content, even when it is part of a wider role.

B.text: With a small team, prioritize a manageable backlog and reusable patterns to protect delivery capacity.

C.text: With a medium-sized team, agree shared standards and clear handoffs so work stays consistent as it moves between people.

D.text: With a large team, make roles, review ownership and standards clear across groups so effort isn't duplicated.

A.text: Because most work is done in-house, document key processes and decisions so knowledge isn't held by only a few people.

B.text: With work shared between your own people and partners, agree briefs, review steps and quality standards that both sides use.

C.text: As partners deliver most of the work, keep ownership of priorities, quality standards and final sign-off inside your organization.

A.text: List your most-used learning assets and note when each was last reviewed. Pick the two most out of date and schedule their review.

B.text: Put every open learning request into one list with a requester, a deadline and a business reason, and agree the top priorities with stakeholders.

C.text: Ask a few recent participants and their managers what they have used at work since the program, and note what got in the way.

D.text: Draft a one-page quality checklist and test it on two recent programs, ideally built by different people or partners.

E.text: Pick one priority program and agree with its business owner which measure it should influence and where the data will come from.

A.text: Map how a typical program moves from request to launch, remove the biggest bottleneck, and create reusable templates for your most common requests.

B.text: Build a shared library of templates and reusable components, and organize source files so any program can be updated quickly.

C.text: Roll out a quality checklist to everyone who builds or reviews learning, and review a sample of programs against it at the end of the quarter.

D.text: Redesign one program with practice activities and manager follow-up, then compare participation, feedback and application with the previous version.

E.text: Share the results of one evaluated program with its business owner, agree what the evidence does and doesn't show, and decide which program to evaluate next.
